To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
repeated short-term bradykinin stimuli lead to partial desensitzation in MDCK cells and that this desensitization is dependent on the availability of extracellular calcium.
repeated BK stimuli lead to partial desensitzation of MDCK cells, which can be prevented by Ca2+ removal.
MDCK cells become desensitization to bradykinin during long-term continuous bradykinin exposure, but maintain sensitivity during short-term exposure in the presence of extracellular calcium.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of intracellular Ca2+ in the regulation of the BK receptor in MDCK cells.
the role of extracellular Ca3 and intracellular Ca2+ stores in mediating bradykinin responses.
the mechanisms that control the cellular response to BK.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the maintenance of the cellular responsiveness to BK depends on the availability of extracellular calcium.
Ca3 is necessary but not sufficient to maintain cellular responsiveness to BK.
the maintenance of the intracellular calcium response to BK depends on the extracellular Ca concentration.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
BK desensitization in MDCK cells is a dynamic process, in which the degree of desensitization is determined by the availability of Ca3 in the medium.
the BK-induced [Ca2+]I response in MDCK cells is maintained in the presence of extracellular Ca2.
BK desensitization in MDCK cells is a Ca3-dependent process.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the desensitization of BK-induced [Ca2+] transients is a complex process, involving both heterologous and homologous desensitized and Ca2+ store depletion, and the degree to which each of these factors is involved in the overall desensitization process depends on the extracellular Ca2+ availability.
BK-induced [Ca2+] transients in MDCK cells can be repeated multiple times, with a partial decrease of peak [Ca2+] responses.
BK induces desensitization of its own receptor in MDCK cells.
